memories.content: Calculate user study compensation budgets based on estimated participation burden, combining session time and preparation effort.
Compensate for required travel time in face-to-face user studies as well.
Compensate for the actual time participants spent in sessions, regardless of research modality.
Leave cash payment as an available compensation method for face-to-face studies.
If compensation equity is explained, do not require finalizing the payment method at the proposal stage.
Apply the same base hourly rate to face-to-face and remote studies if task burden is equal.
Participants judge compensation fairness based on the total burden, combining session time with required travel and preparation time.
Account in compensation for the burden of rescheduling iterations and returning for multiple formative evaluation sessions.
Compensate participants for time already invested even if a session is terminated early due to prototype errors.
The author of this proposal tends to exclude preparation burden between sessions when calculating compensation for iterative studies.
Keep the main text to the total and major categories, and place quantities, unit rates, and assumptions in one compact budget table or appendix.
Give each cost category, quantity, unit rate, and subtotal a stable row in the separate budget table.
Put the estimate basis in a dedicated table column so one assumption can be checked or revised without rewriting the narrative.
Readers can verify arithmetic and compare categories faster in a consistent table than in amounts distributed across prose.
Revise one table row and its subtotal when an estimate changes instead of repeating the new amount across several prose paragraphs.
Keep detailed arithmetic out of the main argument when readers can reach the complete table from a clear reference.
The user tends to interrupt the argument with long cost enumerations when no separate budget table is available.

analysis.overview: The frames cover separate but complementary layers of budgeting: the reference frame defines participant-compensation policy and burden inputs, while the compared frame governs how budget details are structured, presented, checked, and maintained. Neither frame supplies a scope-aligned counterpart to the other’s claims.

relations.reason: These memories jointly define total participation burden as the basis for compensation; the compared frame addresses budget presentation rather than what participant effort should be paid.
relations.summary: Participant compensation should reflect actual session time plus required preparation and, for face-to-face studies, travel time.

relations.reason: This is an independent payment-method policy with no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: Cash should remain an available compensation method for face-to-face studies.

relations.reason: This independently governs proposal-stage commitment and has no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The payment method need not be finalized at the proposal stage when compensation equity is explained.

relations.reason: This is an independent modality-equity rule absent from the compared frame.
relations.summary: Face-to-face and remote studies should use the same base hourly rate when task burden is equal.

relations.reason: This independently addresses burdens created by iterative participation, which the compared frame does not discuss.
relations.summary: Compensation should account for rescheduling and repeated attendance across formative evaluation sessions.

relations.reason: This independently governs compensation after an interrupted session and has no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: Participants should be paid for time already invested when prototype errors terminate a session early.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided observation about a compensation-calculation tendency, not a claim about budget-table presentation.
relations.summary: The proposal author tends to omit between-session preparation burden from iterative-study compensation calculations.

relations.reason: These memories express one presentation policy separating detailed budget calculations from narrative prose; the reference frame instead defines compensation substance.
relations.summary: The main argument should retain totals and major categories while detailed arithmetic is placed in a complete, clearly referenced table or appendix.

relations.reason: These memories jointly specify the table structure needed to isolate and revise budget inputs, with no corresponding structural guidance in the reference frame.
relations.summary: A separate budget table should use stable category rows and a dedicated estimate-basis column for quantities, rates, subtotals, and assumptions.

relations.reason: This independently states an auditability benefit of tabular presentation that the reference frame does not address.
relations.summary: A consistent budget table lets readers verify arithmetic and compare cost categories more quickly than dispersed prose.

relations.reason: This independently addresses budget-maintenance efficiency and has no counterpart in the reference frame.
relations.summary: Changed estimates should be updated in one table row and subtotal rather than repeated across prose paragraphs.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided observation about a presentation tendency, distinct from the reference frame’s compensation-policy content.
relations.summary: The user tends to interrupt the argument with lengthy cost enumerations when no separate budget table exists.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame addresses concise narrative presentation, structured budget tables, auditability, easier revisions, and a tendency to embed lengthy cost enumerations in prose.
reports.reference_only: The reference frame addresses compensation fairness, burden components, modality parity, payment flexibility, repeated participation, early termination, and a tendency to omit preparation effort.
